question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)?$

I. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,-1)$

II. ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ is defined
question.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x-y}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{x-y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x-y}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,-1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0-(-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,-1) & =\frac{1}{0-(-1)}=\frac{1}{1}=1 \\ {f}_{y}(0,-1) & =-\frac{1}{0-(-1)}=-\frac{1}{1}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0-1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0).
$$

which is also undefined. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".
